opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd describe my competitive programming record as solid but not top-tier. There were people around me who were much more talented, the ones who seemed to see the solution almost instantly. I wasn't one of them. I got my results mostly by putting in a lot of time, grinding through problems, and learning from my mistakes.

Looking back, the medals and rankings aren't what I value most. What stayed with me was the training. Competitive programming teaches you to break a hard problem into pieces, think carefully about complexity and edge cases, and write correct code under pressure. Those habits turned out to be very useful later, in research and especially in systems work, where performance and correctness really matter.

It also taught me how to handle failure. You can prepare for months and still have a bad day at a contest. Learning to accept that, figure out what went wrong, and keep going has probably mattered more to me than any particular result.

So I'm grateful for that period. It wasn't the peak of what I've done, but it gave me a foundation, and a lot of the friends I made through it are still people I learn from today.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try to keep a pretty sober view of it. I did competitive programming for a long time, starting in high school with the olympiad circuit in China and then through university with ICPC. I got some medals, I had some good years, and I'm proud of that. But I don't think of those results as the achievement itself. The achievement is more what the training did to me.

The thing competitive programming gives you is a very specific kind of discipline. You sit with a problem that looks impossible, you break it down, you find the structure hiding underneath, and you have to get it exactly right, not approximately right, under time pressure. Doing that thousands of times rewires how you think. When I later moved into systems work and started building things like SGLang, I noticed that the instinct to look for the real bottleneck and to reason carefully about complexity came straight from those years.

At the same time, I'm aware of the limits. Contests reward a narrow skill. They don't teach you how to work with people, how to pick problems that matter, or how to keep a project alive for years. A lot of very strong competitive programmers never translate it into anything beyond the contest, and a lot of great engineers and researchers never competed at all. So I'd say my results were good, maybe better than I expected when I started, but the real value was the foundation, not the ranking. I'm more interested in what I've been able to build on top of it than in the medals themselves.

Those are valuable skills, but they’re not the same as knowing which problems are worth solving. So I’d assess my achievements in that context: something to be proud of, but also a foundation to build on.
